title: 3 Enoch (The Book of the Palaces)

stories.title: 📜 3 Enoch (The Book of the Palaces)
summaryBullets: Rabbi Ishmael ascends in a vision to the heavenly palaces (hekhalot).
He beholds the Merkabah, the divine chariot, surrounded by angelic hosts.
The angel Metatron, formerly Enoch son of Jared, greets him as guide.
God transforms Enoch into the angel Metatron, the Prince of the Presence.
Metatron is given robes of glory, a crown, and a throne next to God.
Angels protest his exaltation, but God defends His choice of Enoch.
Metatron is granted authority over angelic hosts and cosmic orders.
Metatron shows Ishmael the ranks of angels, seraphim, cherubim, and ophanim.
Descriptions of fiery beings, their voices like thunder, and their service around God’s throne.
Angels who sinned are imprisoned, awaiting judgment.
Metatron is depicted as commander of heavenly hosts under God’s authority.
Enoch sees the heavenly court assembled, with thrones of judgment set.
Books of record are opened before the Ancient of Days.
Angels testify concerning the deeds of humans and of nations.
Metatron oversees the angelic scribes recording works for judgment.
Rabbi Ishmael is shown the Merkabah chariot in detail.
Fiery wheels (ophanim) move with the spirit, covered in eyes.
Cherubim and seraphim sing praises without ceasing.
The throne of glory shines with indescribable brilliance.
Metatron reveals to Ishmael the mysteries of creation and order of the cosmos.
The structure of heavens, earth, seas, and underworld are explained.
Laws governing stars, seasons, and spirits are disclosed.
The balance of light and darkness, good and evil, is set by God’s decree.
Metatron is entrusted with divine names and seals of power.
He is declared lesser Yahweh by some angels, though always subordinate to God.
Divine mysteries of names are used for sustaining creation and judgment.
List of Metatron’s many names and titles is given.
He is called Prince of the Presence, Youth, Lesser Yahweh, and more.
Each name reflects an aspect of his role as exalted servant of God.
crossRefs: Genesis 5:21-24: Enoch walked with God after the birth of Methuselah, and he was not, for God took him, the two sentences this entire book is an expansion of.
Hebrews 11:5: By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God, which is all the New Testament says about that removal.

Ezekiel 1:4-28: The vision by the river Chebar of four living creatures, wheels beside them, an expanse like crystal and a throne like sapphire with a figure of fire and gleaming metal above it, the vision this whole body of writing is built on.
Ezekiel 10:9-22: The wheels are named as whirling ones and the living creatures of the first vision are identified as cherubim, which is where the ranks of angels this book parades get their names.

Daniel 7:9-10: Thrones are set in place, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, a river of fire flows out before him, thousand thousands serve him, the court sits in judgment and the books are opened, the scene this book stages at length.

Isaiah 6:1-4: Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne high and lifted up, the train of his robe filling the temple, and the seraphim above it with six wings each calling to one another, the only place in Scripture that names them.

Exodus 23:20-21: God sends an angel ahead of Israel and warns them to obey his voice and not rebel, because he will not pardon their transgression, for my name is in him; this book quotes that last clause outright as its warrant for the title it gives Metatron.

Deuteronomy 6:4: Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one, the confession behind the punishment this book records when a rabbi looks at Metatron enthroned and says there are two powers in heaven.

translationNotes.note: The Book of the Palaces, the Hebrew title. A hekhal is the great hall of a palace, and it is the word used of the main room of the temple, the space standing in front of the Most Holy Place, as at Ezekiel 41:1. In this literature the hekhalot are the halls a visionary passes through in order before he reaches the throne. The name 3 Enoch is not ancient; Hugo Odeberg coined it for his Cambridge edition of 1928.

Chariot. The word does not appear in Ezekiel 1 at all; Ezekiel describes living creatures and wheels and never calls the whole apparatus a chariot. Scripture applies the word to the throne exactly once, at 1 Chronicles 28:18, where David hands Solomon the plan for the golden cherubim that spread their wings over the ark and calls them the chariot. Maaseh Merkavah, the work of the chariot, is the rabbinic name for study of that vision.

Ishmael ben Elisha, a teacher of the early second century AD and one of the Tannaim, the first generation of named rabbinic authorities. He is the speaker throughout this book, not Enoch, which is why the manuscripts also head it the Book of Rabbi Ishmael the High Priest. Enoch appears only as the angel who meets him at the top.

The angel who guides Ishmael and the figure the book is really about. He tells Ishmael that he was Enoch son of Jared before God took him and remade him into fire. Where the name comes from has never been established, and the book itself does not say. What it does say is that everything he holds was handed to him: the throne, the crown, the robes and the authority, with God answering the angels who object rather than Metatron answering them.

The most contested title in the book. Chapter 12 has God call him the lesser YHWH before the whole heavenly household and gives the warrant in the same breath: as it is written, for my name is in him. That clause is Exodus 23:21, said of the angel God sends ahead of Israel. Deuteronomy 6:4 and Isaiah 45:5 are the sentences the title has to be read alongside.

Chapter 16 has Elisha ben Abuyah, called Aher, the Other, come up to see the chariot, fix his eyes on Metatron seated, and say that there are two powers in heaven. A voice from heaven answers with Jeremiah 3:22, Return, O backsliding children, and excepts him by name. Then the angel Aniyel is sent to give Metatron sixty lashes of fire and make him stand on his feet. He is made to stand, and after that he does not sit.

Chapter 3 has Metatron say he has seventy names, matched to the seventy tongues of the world, and the manuscripts print the list. Seventy is the count of nations in the table at Genesis 10, and it is the number of elders Moses is told to gather at Numbers 11:16 so that they may bear the burden of the people with him.

Literally prince of the face. The title marks an angel admitted to stand before the throne rather than one sent out on errands. Isaiah 63:9 speaks of the angel of his presence, literally the angel of his face, saving Israel. Luke 1:19 has Gabriel state the same standing in Greek: I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God.

Burning ones, from saraph, to burn. Isaiah 6:2-6 is the only place in Scripture they appear: six wings each, two covering the face, two covering the feet, two for flying, and one of them takes a live coal from the altar with tongs. The same root gives the fiery serpents of Numbers 21:6-8, which is why the word can carry both senses.

Not winged infants. Genesis 3:24 stations them east of Eden with a flaming sword turning every way to guard the way to the tree of life. Exodus 25:18-22 has two of them hammered out of one piece of gold, facing each other with wings over the mercy seat, and God speaks from between them. Ezekiel 10:20 identifies the living creatures of the first vision as cherubim.

Wheels, from ofan, a wheel. Ezekiel 1:15-21 sets a wheel beside each living creature, a wheel within a wheel, going straight forward without swivelling, rising when the creatures rise because the spirit of the living creature is in the wheels. Ezekiel 1:18 gives the rims full of eyes all round. In this literature the wheels are a rank of angels rather than machinery.

The word at Ezekiel 1:4 for the glowing thing in the middle of the fire, and again at Ezekiel 1:27 for the appearance from the waist up. English versions render it gleaming metal, amber or electrum, and nobody has established what substance it names. Modern Hebrew took the word over for electricity. In this literature the hashmallim are treated as another rank of angels.

The curtain hung before the throne. Metatron shows Ishmael the curtain spread in front of the Holy One with every generation of the world graven on it, everything they have done and everything they will do to the end. The word is a loan into Hebrew for a heavy hanging. The temple had a curtain doing the same work of shutting off the presence, made to the specification at Exodus 26:31-33.

The name this literature gives the highest heaven, where the throne stands. It comes from Psalm 68:4, which calls on Israel to lift up a song to him who rides through the aravot, a word English versions render clouds, deserts or heavens. Paul reports a man caught up to the third heaven at 2 Corinthians 12:2, which is the only place Scripture puts a number on one.

The three angels who object when Enoch is exalted and bring formal charges against him in the high heavens. The same names belong to the angels who came down and taught men sorcery in the older Enoch material. Genesis 6:1-4 is the passage all of it grows out of, the sons of God taking wives of the daughters of men, and Jude 1:6 speaks of angels who did not keep their own domain and are held in chains under darkness.

The presence of God as it settles into a place. The noun itself is not in the Hebrew Bible; it is built from the verb shakan, to dwell or to pitch a tent, which is everywhere. Exodus 25:8 has God tell Israel to make him a sanctuary so that he may dwell among them, and Exodus 40:34-35 has the cloud cover the tent and the glory fill the tabernacle so heavily that Moses cannot go in.

stories.keyTakeaway: Rabbi Ishmael is taken up through the heavenly palaces and met by an angel who tells him that he was Enoch son of Jared before God took him. The book gives that angel, Metatron, a throne, a crown, seventy names and the title lesser YHWH, records the protest of the angels at his exaltation, and then works outward through the ranks of seraphim, cherubim and ophanim, the court with the books of record open, the ordering of stars and seasons, and the divine names entrusted to him.

intro:
3 Enoch is the Hebrew Enoch. Its Hebrew title is Sefer Hekhalot (ספר היכלות), the Book of the Palaces, from hekhal, the great hall of a palace or of the temple. Manuscripts also head it the Book of Rabbi Ishmael the High Priest. The name 3 Enoch is not ancient; Hugo Odeberg coined it for his edition and English translation published at Cambridge in 1928, the first critical text, which divides the work into forty-eight chapters with further material attached in some manuscripts as 48B, 48C, and 48D.

The speaker is not Enoch but Rabbi Ishmael ben Elisha, a teacher of the early second century AD. He ascends to the heavenly palaces, sees the Merkabah, the throne-chariot of Ezekiel 1, and is met by an angel who guides him and who tells him that he was Enoch son of Jared before God took him and transformed him into Metatron, Prince of the Presence. The book gives Metatron a throne, a crown, and robes of glory, records the protest of the angels at his exaltation, lists his many names and titles, and describes him as the appointed scribe over the recording angels. It then works outward: the ranks of seraphim, cherubim, and ophanim; the heavenly court seated with the books of record open before the Ancient of Days; the ordering of stars, seasons, and spirits; and the divine names entrusted to Metatron. One of the titles the text applies to him is the lesser YHWH.

3 Enoch belongs to Hekhalot literature, the body of Hebrew and Aramaic texts on the palaces and the chariot that includes Hekhalot Rabbati, Hekhalot Zutarti, Maaseh Merkavah, and Shiur Qomah, and it travels with them in the manuscripts. That is why its dating question is a different question from the one asked of 1 and 2 Enoch. 1 Enoch is attested in Aramaic copies made before the Christian era and found at Qumran; 2 Enoch is attested in Coptic fragments and in Slavonic copies. 3 Enoch has no ancient manuscript at all. It survives in medieval Hebrew codices of the Hekhalot corpus, of which Peter Schafer printed the principal witnesses in parallel in his Synopse zur Hekhalot-Literatur in 1981, and its language is a late rabbinic Hebrew carrying Greek and Latin loanwords. The dating proposals name different layers. (1) Hugo Odeberg, in 1928, assigned the main body, chapters 3 to 48A, to the second half of the third century AD, judged chapters 3 to 15 to rest on material from the first or second century, and placed chapters 1 and 2 and the appendices later. (2) Gershom Scholem, in his studies of Merkabah mysticism from 1941 onward, argued that the Hekhalot writings as a whole belong to the Talmudic period and to rabbinic circles rather than to medieval mysticism. (3) Philip Alexander, who translated the book for The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha in 1983, places the final redaction in the fifth or sixth century AD, in or near Babylonia.

The book is not a canon-list text. No communion receives it as canonical, and it appears in no ancient list of scriptures; it was copied and preserved inside Jewish mystical collections.
